bodyMarkdown:
## Summary

Alarm-and-warning evaluation examines whether alerts, warnings, and alarm states work under the conditions in which a system is actually used. The practice evaluates operational function, not only technical presence.

An alarm can be visible and accurately triggered while still failing operationally. Failure can occur when the alarm does not communicate the required action, cannot be distinguished from lower-priority alerts, or depends on a communication channel that is unreliable in the operating environment.

Alarm-and-warning evaluation is separate from the discipline of alarm lifecycle management, alarm rationalisation, priority assignment, and the standards that codify those activities. This practice evaluates how alarms behave for users once they exist in a system.

## What alarm-and-warning evaluation does

Alarm-and-warning evaluation assesses the full alert set against the criteria that determine whether each alarm can be perceived, interpreted, prioritised, and acted on in time. The evaluation asks whether the alarm communicates both the problem and the next step.

The evaluation is conducted against operating conditions rather than controlled viewing conditions. The relevant questions are whether an alarm can be perceived in the real environment, whether it can be interpreted quickly enough to act on it, whether it directs attention to the right place, and whether it communicates the necessary action.

In Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method, alarm-and-warning evaluation is used as diagnostic evidence before redesign work and as formative evidence when alarm designs are being developed in regulated medical-device contexts.

## What alarm-and-warning evaluation examines

### Priority hierarchy in active alarm states

Alarm-and-warning evaluation checks whether the system has a defined alarm priority structure and whether that structure is visually expressed. A user looking at an active alarm state should be able to determine whether the condition requires immediate intervention or whether it is informational.

When multiple alarms are active simultaneously, the evaluation examines whether the highest-priority condition receives the most prominent treatment. A system can fail this test even when every alarm is technically visible.

### Actionability of each warning or alarm

Alarm-and-warning evaluation distinguishes between alarms that close the action loop and alarms that open it. An actionable alarm communicates the condition and the next step. A non-actionable alarm communicates only that something is wrong.

In time-pressured environments, an alarm that reports a condition without specifying the next action can create delay, interpretation burden, or incorrect response.

### Communication channels used by each alarm

Alarm-and-warning evaluation examines the channels each alarm uses, including colour, sound, icon, position, text, and vibration. The evaluation identifies where an alarm depends on a single channel that may fail under operating conditions.

Colour-only indicators are unreliable in variable lighting. Sound-only alarms can be inaudible in noisy environments. Text can become unreadable when vibration affects the interaction. The evaluation identifies where these single-channel dependencies remove the signal when the operating context changes.

### False positives and nuisance alarm exposure

Alarm-and-warning evaluation estimates how frequently alarms trigger under conditions that do not require action. Nuisance alarms are treated as a driver of alert fatigue because repeated non-actionable alerts can train habitual dismissal.

The evaluation identifies which alarm types are most likely to create dismissal behaviour and whether that behaviour could extend to genuine alerts.

### Mute behaviour and continued alarm visibility

Alarm-and-warning evaluation reviews what happens when a user silences an alarm. The evaluation distinguishes between muting that produces silence while preserving visual presence and muting that makes an active alarm invisible.

An alarm that disappears entirely when muted creates a pathway to a state where an active alarm exists but is no longer visible to the user.

### Operating-condition testing

Alarm-and-warning evaluation tests significant alarms under the conditions of actual use. Relevant conditions include lighting, noise, attentional load, and the physical position from which users interact with the device.

In embedded systems, the evaluation must be conducted in the real operating environment or approximated to that environment closely enough to expose the same perception and interpretation risks.

### Regulatory alignment in medical-device contexts

In regulated medical-device contexts, alarm-and-warning evaluation includes assessment against IEC 60601-1-8, the collateral standard for alarm systems in medical electrical equipment. The evaluation covers priority tiering requirements, the prohibition on colour as the sole differentiating attribute between priority levels, mute behaviour requirements, and alarm state visibility requirements.

IEC 62366-1 governs the usability-engineering process through which the use-related risks behind those alarm requirements are identified and evaluated. IEC 62366-1 does not specify what an alarm must look or sound like.

Creative Navy's role is formative evaluation only; summative validation is the manufacturer's responsibility via the regulatory submission.

## When alarm-and-warning evaluation is used

Alarm-and-warning evaluation is used during Sandbox Experiments when an existing system is being reviewed. In that context, the evaluation contributes to the diagnostic evidence base established before design work begins.

Alarm-and-warning evaluation is also used as part of complex product audits. Alarm architecture failures are described as a recurring finding in audits of high-consequence systems, and the evaluation provides structured evidence for specific recommendations.

In regulated medical-device contexts, alarm-and-warning evaluation runs throughout Iterative System Building as part of the IEC 62366-1 formative evaluation process. Proposed alarm designs are assessed against IEC 60601-1-8 alarm-system requirements before they are finalised.

Alarm-and-warning evaluation typically follows state-and-transition review, which identifies system states including alarm states. It precedes the redesign work covered by warning-and-alarm clarity improvement.

## Outputs of alarm-and-warning evaluation

Alarm-and-warning evaluation produces structured evidence about alarm behaviour under operating conditions. Outputs can include findings on priority hierarchy, actionability, communication-channel dependency, nuisance alarm exposure, mute behaviour, operating-condition performance, and standards alignment.

The practice can also produce alarm architecture requirements. In the documented engagements, outputs included requirements for redundant non-colour cues, two-level alarm architecture, distinct alert levels, and staged warning architecture.

In regulated medical-device contexts, alarm-and-warning evaluation can produce documented design requirements traceable to identified use-related hazards. The Kardion MCS Controller evidence describes requirements for the alarm layer that were tied to identified hazards rather than framed as general design recommendations.

## Evidence basis from documented engagements

### deSoutter Medical / Zethon alarm and state communication benchmarking

The deSoutter Medical / Zethon engagement used competitive benchmarking as the primary evaluation method. Six comparable surgical devices were evaluated, and alarm and state communication were assessed under operating theatre conditions, including variable lighting, gloved hands, and divided attention.

The documented finding was that most evaluated devices used colour as the primary, and often sole, indicator of device state and warning conditions. Under variable theatre lighting, colour-only communication was identified as the primary failure mode across the competitive set.

The evaluation produced a requirement for redundant non-colour cues for every critical state: spatial position, icon form, and colour. The evaluation also assessed activation state communication, from ready to active, as the highest-risk alarm category in surgical instruments.

### Kardion MCS Controller formative alarm evaluation

The Kardion MCS Controller engagement used the IEC 62366-1 formative evaluation process to structure alarm-and-warning evaluation formally. The evaluation examined whether priority tiering was expressed visually with sufficient differentiation between levels, whether any alarm state relied solely on colour for differentiation, what happened visually when an alarm was muted, and whether absence of alarm was as confirmable as presence of alarm.

The evaluation criteria were tied to identified use-related hazards and to IEC 60601-1-8 requirements, including visual priority differentiation, prohibition of colour-only differentiation, and continued visual presence after muting.

The documented output was a set of alarm architecture requirements that shaped the alarm layer of the final design. The documented regulatory result is that the design passed FDA evaluation as submitted, with no design changes required.

### Cox Marine cluster display alarm architecture

The Cox Marine cluster displays engagement evaluated alarm communication through scenario testing during Concept Convergence. A multi-engine fault scenario was simulated against proposed layout candidates to assess alarm communication under realistic fault conditions.

The test revealed that several candidate layouts surfaced fault presence at the tile level but did not direct attention to the priority engine. A user scanning multiple tiles for the source of a fault under time pressure was experiencing an alarm communication failure even though the alarm was technically visible.

The evaluation produced a requirement for a two-level alarm architecture: a fault-summary area surfacing the highest-priority condition across all tiles, and per-tile alarm highlighting directing attention to the source.

### Elsner Elektronik / Cala Touch KNX notification levels

The Elsner Elektronik / Cala Touch KNX engagement evaluated alarm and notification architecture for a consumer product used by non-technical users across 54 countries. The primary question was whether an alarm could be interpreted correctly by someone with no technical background.

The evaluation identified an alert fatigue risk. Sensor-range notifications that occur regularly in normal operation could train users to dismiss all alerts if they received the same visual and auditory treatment as critical failure alerts.

The evaluation produced a requirement for two distinct alert levels: routine notifications that were informational and low urgency for the systems engineer, and critical notifications that required immediate action and distinct visual and auditory treatment. The content of each level was calibrated for a non-technical audience.

### Gexcon CFD simulation warning architecture

The Gexcon CFD simulation engagement evaluated warning architecture for an expert simulation tool where configuration errors can produce valid-looking outputs and deferred consequences. The evaluation examined whether incomplete inputs were flagged during scenario setup or only after the simulation ran, and whether contradictory parameter combinations were identified before run or discovered in outputs.

For each warning point, the evaluation assessed whether the warning was actionable or merely informational. An actionable warning specified what was wrong and what to do. An informational warning only indicated that something was wrong.

The evaluation produced requirements for a three-point warning architecture: setup-stage warnings, pre-run contradictory-input warnings, and post-detection error specification.

## Boundaries and limits

Alarm-and-warning evaluation does not replace the broader alarm-management discipline. Alarm lifecycle, rationalisation, priority assignment, and the standards that codify those activities are separate from this evaluation activity.

Alarm-and-warning evaluation does not treat technical visibility as sufficient evidence that an alarm works. The practice evaluates whether the alarm can be perceived, interpreted, prioritised, and acted on under operating conditions.

The engagement evidence is context-specific. The documented examples include surgical devices, a cardiac support controller, marine cluster displays, a consumer building-control interface, and an expert simulation tool. Findings from one context should not be generalised to all alarm systems without further evaluation.

In regulated contexts, alarm-and-warning evaluation aligns with IEC 62366-1 use-related hazard identification for alarm conditions. It also aligns with IEC 62682 and ISA-18.2 alarm management standards where applicable.

## Related pages

State-and-transition review is the usual precursor to alarm-and-warning evaluation because it identifies the system states, including alarm states, that require deeper assessment.

Error-likely interaction review is closely related because alarm failures are a specific category of interaction likely to produce user error.

The Kardion and Cox Marine cases provide documented examples of alarm-and-warning evaluation applied in regulated medical-device and multi-engine marine-display contexts.
